carousels.title: The one-session time audit
carousels.caption: A clock tells you the total. An audit helps you ask what happened. Use these four categories once, then choose one practical delay to investigate. Rest is not automatically wasted time. No time-saving result is promised.
slides: WHERE DID THE HOUR GO?
A one-session audit for your next gym visit.
LOG FOUR BUCKETS
Lifting / Rest / Setup / Waiting. Use your own minutes, not somebody else's example.
FIND ONE DELAY
Which practical issue can you change? Repeated trips for forgotten equipment are one possibility.
KEEP THE CONTEXT
Do not cut every rest period. Note how busy the gym was and what else changed.
COMPARE, THEN ASK
Try one practical change. Compare several sessions. What question does your log raise?

carousels.title: A useful exercise-swap question
carousels.caption: A muscle label is only part of the question. Write down the goal and constraint before discussing an alternative with a qualified coach. This checklist is not a universal exercise-swap prescription.
slides: MACHINE TAKEN?
Prepare a better question before your next crowded session.
1 / NAME THE PURPOSE
Are you practicing a particular lift, or pursuing another training goal? Write it down.
2 / NAME THE CONSTRAINT
What equipment is available? Which movements do you already know? What changed today?
3 / DISCUSS THE CHOICE
Use that context with a qualified coach. A matching muscle label does not establish equivalence.
SAVE YOUR PLAN B
Record the agreed option and its context. Review it when your goal or constraints change.

carousels.title: Three checks for a fitness chart
carousels.caption: These examples teach chart reading, not training outcomes. A percentage, an axis, and a sample count can all change your first impression. Keep the underlying comparison visible.
slides: A BIG NUMBER NEEDS CONTEXT
Three checks before a fitness chart changes your mind.
CHECK THE BASELINE
Invented example: 2 to 3 = +50%, but also +1 point. What does a point mean?
CHECK THE AXIS
Invented scores: 90 and 100. Starting the scale at 80 changes the picture, not the scores.
CHECK THE UNIT
People, limbs, sets and sessions are different counts. What is the study's unit of comparison?
ASK FOR THE OUTCOME
Better at what, compared with what, and measured over how long?

carousels.title: Your next session, one useful question
carousels.caption: Choose one question you can observe. Keep the goal, constraints and context visible. A personal log can guide the next question; it does not prove a universal training rule.
slides: ONE SESSION. ONE QUESTION.
Choose a practical question before changing everything.
TIME QUESTION
Which delay can I change? Log lifting, rest, setup and waiting separately.
EQUIPMENT QUESTION
What should this exercise accomplish? Prepare a Plan B question around that purpose.
EVIDENCE QUESTION
Who was studied, what was compared, and which outcome changed?
KEEP A SMALL RECORD
What happened? What else was different? What should I investigate next?

stories.question: Which part makes your session run long?
stories.followup: If it's rest, keep its purpose in view. A delay and recovery are different questions.

stories.question: A score rises from 2 to 3. What changed?
stories.followup: Both +1 point and +50% describe this invented example. The baseline matters.

stories.question: What most often forces an exercise swap?
stories.followup: Keep the original goal visible before choosing the alternative.

stories.question: 8 people, each with 2 legs studied. How many people?
stories.followup: Eight. Paired limbs do not become sixteen independent participants.

stories.question: What do you read first on a chart?
stories.followup: Read both. A close-up can be useful, but the scale needs to stay visible.

stories.question: One better session proves the change worked?
stories.followup: Not by itself. Keep notes on other changes and compare more sessions.

stories.question: Which series should go deeper?
stories.followup: A reply explaining the problem you face is especially useful. Do not share private health details.

stories.question: Would you use a one-session audit?
stories.followup: If you tried it, what did you notice? No particular improvement is expected.
